units: a sports coach notices that beginners are short of breath after a single flight of stairs
a seated life weakens the breathing quietly
the heart muscle settles for reduced effort
the vessels become less elastic
night rest deteriorates in bodies that are little used
the coach advises brisk walks repeated across the week
these walks include moderate climbs
late-afternoon weariness lessens after this practice
text: At a neighbourhood training hall, the coach watches whoever comes through the door. Most of them arrive winded after one flight of stairs, and he knows exactly why. A seated life wears the breathing machinery down quietly, without ever announcing itself. Let a still spell run on and the heart muscle settles for the smallest effort it can get away with, the vessels stiffen and lose their spring, and the shortest run turns punishing. He points to a quieter consequence as well. Sleep frays, because a body asked for nothing never demands deep repair. His remedy stays modest: a brisk walk, taken again and again across the week, broken up by gentle climbs. The results show quickly. Breathing lengthens, the late-afternoon slump loosens its grip, and the mood clears. Nothing dramatic here, an ordinary cause, an ordinary correction, a chain running backwards.

units: evenings have been overrun by lit screens
falling asleep is pushed later and later
the writer refuses to blame the devices themselves
the writer blames the lack of a limit fixed in advance
he recommends choosing a stopping hour before the evening
he advises leaving the device outside the bedroom
he suggests replacing that habit with quiet reading
he holds that the mildness of a rule is what makes it last
text: Our evenings have filled up with lit screens until they overflow. Night falls, the eye fastens on a cold brightness, thought dissolves in it, and sleep slips back half an hour, then another. I distrust the easy charge. The harm does not sit inside the device, it sits in the missing boundary, the one nobody drew while tiredness had yet to take our judgement away. A blunt ban would collapse, as savage diets collapse. What I argue for is gentler, and negotiated with oneself. Settle on a stopping hour at midday, while the mind still reasons. Leave the thing outside the bedroom, so that reaching for it costs something. Put slow reading in place of the electric vigil, a low conversation, a stretch. Sleep is never rescued by heroic denial, only by a mild rule you keep without noticing that you keep it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a rehabilitation therapist has worked with back patients since the start of his career
he contrasts two profiles among those who consult him
the first profile carries heavy loads and shows tightened muscles
the second profile stays seated and lacks muscular tone
both profiles complain of a comparable discomfort
he treats the first with stretching and heat
he treats the second with strengthening built up by degrees
he refuses to apply the same protocol to both cases
text: The therapist working out of this practice has sorted back patients into two profiles since his first year, and every examination opens with that question. One kind lifts heavy loads most of the week: the muscles sit rigid, the shoulders lock, the neck feels hard under the hand. The other kind stays parked in front of a screen: the fibres go slack, the posture caves, the abdominal girdle holds nothing up any more. Both describe the same low ache, and people conclude from that a single treatment would serve. He argues the opposite. For the first he prescribes graded stretching, heat, and a release led by the breath, so that a clenched back loosens again. For the second he insists on strengthening built up by degrees, without which no relief holds. One symptom, he says, hiding two opposite mechanics.

units: a cookery book meant for people recovering from illness is examined
the reviewer approves of the plainness of the preparations
the recipes limit fats and long cooking
the book offers pairings rich in protein
the portions are suited to a weakened appetite
the explanations about chewing are judged useful
the review faults the absence of guidance on keeping food
the conclusion nevertheless recommends the book for family kitchens
text: This collection of dishes for those recovering from illness deserves close attention, so sharply do its choices cut against the usual output. Three merits stand out. Plainness first: the author sets aside endless cooking and heavy fats in favour of plates a weakened stomach takes without protest. Balance next: every pairing brings together a source of protein and a tender vegetable, which gives a nourishing whole that never sits heavily. The portions come sized for a faltering appetite. Instruction last: the pages given over to chewing are worth more than many a longer treatise. One reservation remains. Nothing at all is said about keeping dishes cooked ahead of time, a regrettable gap for readers whose strength is low. The book stays worth recommending to any family kitchen with recovery in mind.

units: the writer of the message writes to someone close to give news
a shivering fit appeared at the end of the week
a consultation took place the following day
the carer ruled out any complication
three nights of extended rest were prescribed
a hot drink and a light soup made up the whole diet
the fever fell before the end of the treatment
the writer promises a visit as soon as he has recovered
text: I am writing from my bed, and nothing here should worry you. It began at the end of the week. A shivering fit caught me while I was tidying the kitchen, and I went to lie down feverish, unable to finish my own sentence. The following day the carer at the nearby health centre examined me thoroughly. She ruled out any complication and ordered three nights of strict rest, which I accepted without argument. The first two dragged. My whole diet was a warm infusion and a thin soup, and I dropped off as soon as the light went. Then the fever broke all at once, before the course of treatment had finished, and hunger returned like a friend who had left in a temper. I can walk the corridor now without leaning on the wall. I shall come round the moment this tiredness finally releases me.

units: the person questioned explains night-time sweating
an overheated bedroom prevents the inner temperature from dropping
that drop is what allows a proper falling asleep
the body makes up for it by producing sweat
wakings multiply because of that discomfort
the next day's tiredness follows from those interruptions
the speaker advises turning the bedroom heating down
she recommends natural fabrics rather than synthetic ones
text: You want to know why the pillow is soaked every night when you have done nothing to earn it. One sentence covers it: your bedroom is too warm. Here is the mechanism. To drop off properly your body must shed a fraction of a degree of its own heat, and if the surrounding air prevents that, it brings out the heavy weaponry and sets you sweating. So what? So you wake clammy, shove the cover off, drag it back, and the whole pantomime chops your sleep into useless pieces. Hence the heaviness of the morning, without your having stayed up late. What can you actually do about it? Turn the heating down well before bed, and let the room cool by itself. Change the bedding too: natural cloth carries the damp away, synthetics press it against the skin. Give it a week and you will notice the difference.

units: a reception nurse describes the crowding in an emergency department
most of the arrivals concern complaints of no seriousness
seriously ill patients wait longer because of that crowding
the doctor in charge points to ignorance of the other options available
a telephone line giving guidance has been set up
walk-in surgeries open in the evening
the average wait has come down since those measures
the nurse holds that informing the public must go on
text: The nurse on reception describes a waiting room already full from the moment the doors open. Most of what arrives, she says, is minor, a light sprain, a cough that will not shift, a shallow burn, and those cases push the genuinely threatened patients further down the queue. The doctor in charge of the department agrees, with a qualification. People rarely know what exists outside the hospital, he explains, so they head for the place they can name. Two measures followed. A telephone line now gives guidance before anyone sets off, and walk-in surgeries open in the evening across the area. The average wait has already come down, he notes. The nurse is cooler about it. The room will empty for good on the evening when everyone knows where to turn, she says, and not one single day before.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carers of former times put illnesses down to corrupted air
they advised airing rooms and keeping away from unhealthy places
that explanation rested on observation without proof
the discovery of micro-organisms altered this conception
handwashing was brought into the rooms where care was given
mortality after childbirth fell afterwards
both approaches shared the same mistrust of dirt
the older approach knew nothing of the true source of contagion
text: Before anyone had learnt to look at the invisible, carers blamed the air. A thick smell rising off marshy ground, an unaired lane, a shut room: that, it was believed, was where contagion came from. So windows were opened, herbs were burnt, the low districts were avoided. The instinct was not absurd, only blind to its own reason. Then the magnifying glass showed a tiny population swarming over the fingers, and the whole picture tipped over. A dull instruction, wash your hands between one room and the next, brought the death rate among women who had just given birth down further than any fumigation ever had. Set the two doctrines side by side, honestly. Both mistrusted filth, and both prescribed much the same gestures. But the older one aimed at a shadow, while the later one could at last name what it was fighting.

units: the text describes the effects of immersion in cold water
the skin responds by tightening the vessels near the surface
blood withdraws towards the central organs
breathing quickens abruptly on contact
control of the breath limits that reaction
stimulating substances are released after coming out
heart disorders make the practice inadvisable
a short duration is advised for beginners
text: Immersion in cold water works on three separate levels, and each of them deserves its own account. Circulation comes first. On contact the vessels in the skin tighten, blood withdraws towards the central organs, and pressure rises for a short while. Breathing follows. A reflex gasp arrives the moment you go under, fast and beyond control, and taking charge of the out-breath softens that respiratory panic and makes the exercise workable. The chemical answer comes last: on getting out, the body releases stimulating messengers, which accounts for the reviving effect regular bathers describe. Two precautions frame the whole thing. Any known heart abnormality rules the practice out without medical advice, and a beginner keeps the immersion very short, never alone, never after a heavy meal.

units: a librarian suffered from pain in her wrists
she put the pain down at first to her age
a colleague pointed out the unsuitable height of her work surface
an ergonomist examined her workstation
the seat and the screen were raised
regular breaks were brought into her day
the pain went away after several weeks
she then urged the same course on her colleagues
text: The woman in charge of the town library endured a dull ache in both wrists for two seasons, and put it down at first to her age and to ordinary wear. She carried on shelving, lifting and keying in references, until a younger colleague remarked on the odd height of her sorting surface. An ergonomist was then called in. He measured the workstation, watched how her forearms sat, and gave an opinion without softening it: the seat was too low, the screen too far back, and the neck was paying for the whole imbalance. Both were raised. Short breaks were built into the day at settled intervals. Within some weeks the ache had gone, and not a single tablet had been swallowed. From then on she preached the same procedure to her team with a stubbornness nobody could talk her out of.
